full_text:

Investing.com-- Asian stocks mostly fell on Friday as a global bond selloff pushed long-term U.S. Treasury yields to multi-year highs, weighing on risk appetite, while investors awaited details from talks between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
U.S. stock index futures were largely subdued in Asian trading Friday after Wall Street closed marginally lower overnight.

Surging bond yields weigh on Asia stocks; Nikkei bucks trend
Japan's Nikkei 225 was an outlier, rising 1.3%, while the broader TOPIX gained 1.2%.
Japanese stocks extended gains as technology shares continued to recover after a three-day holiday break, while a weaker yen supported exporters.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng slid nearly 2%, with the Hang Seng TECH sub-index declining more than 2.5%.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.5%.
Mainland Chinese, South Korean and Taiwanese markets were closed for holidays, leaving trading volumes thin across the region.
The pressure on equities came as a sharp selloff in global government bonds pushed borrowing costs higher.
The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield last traded at 5.1852%, after jumping to a 19-year high of 5.2251% in the previous session. The 30-year yield was at 5.4705%, after touching 5.5016%, its highest since 2004.
Japanese government bond yields also climbed, with the 10-year yield rising to 3.115%, its highest since 1996. Australia's 10-year yield rose by a similar amount to 5.408%.
Higher oil prices have reinforced concerns that inflation could remain persistent, strengthening expectations for further monetary tightening.
Brent crude eased slightly on Friday after rising more than 3% in the previous session following a Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia.
The oil surge was tempered after reports showed that the U.S. and Iran were exploring a phased deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. rate futures were pricing a 70% chance of another Federal Reserve rate increase in October, up from about 53% earlier in the week.
Traders await Trump-Xi meeting details
Investors were also assessing the outcome of a meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House on Thursday.
The two sides agreed to extend their trade truce by two months, giving negotiators more time to work on tariffs, Chinese purchases, rare-earth supplies and technology restrictions, according to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
The outcome offered some continuity on trade but left several strategic differences unresolved, keeping investors focused on whether the extended truce can translate into a more durable agreement.
Elsewhere in Asia, Singapore's Straits Times Index edged 0.2% lower.
Futures tied to India's Nifty 50 traded largely flat, indicating a muted open.

title: Oil dips after sharp gains as U.S., Iran reportedly explore Hormuz deal
full_text:
U.S. stocks end flat as traders grapple with hawkish Fed, surge in oil and yields
Investing.com-- Oil prices edged lower in Asian trading Friday as reports that the U.S. and Iran were exploring a phased deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz tempered some supply concerns, although a Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia kept geopolitical risks elevated.
As of 20:33 ET (00:33 GMT), Brent Oil Futures expiring in November fell 0.6% to $105.94 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures slipped 0.8% to $93.86 per barrel.
Both benchmarks had climbed as much as 5% during the previous session before paring gains on reports of the U.S.-Iran talks.
Get premium commodity market insights with InvestingPro -- at 50% off now
Saudi Arabia on Thursday said it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis toward areas including Taif and the Yanbu region on the Red Sea.
The attacks revived concerns about Saudi oil infrastructure and export routes, particularly after earlier damage to the kingdom's East-West pipeline disrupted crude shipments to Yanbu.
The security risks are especially significant because Yanbu is a major Red Sea export hub connected to Saudi Arabia's eastern oil fields. Saudi Arabia has been increasing crude pumping toward Yanbu, but tanker loadings from the port had yet to fully resume.
Meanwhile, reports showed that U.S. and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of the conflict that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran.
The strait has become a central bargaining chip, with both sides reluctant to surrender leverage before securing concessions from the other.
Reuters reported that only 17 commodity vessels crossed the strait over one recent weekend, compared with a pre-war average of about 125 vessels a day, although oil shipments have continued at reduced levels.
U.S. inventory data this week offered a counterweight to the geopolitical supply concerns. Commercial crude stocks rose by 3 million barrels in the week ended Sept. 18, versus analysts' expectations for a 641,000-barrel draw, while gasoline inventories fell 1.7 million barrels and distillates declined 400,000 barrels.
Diesel markets also remained in focus after U.S. fuel prices climbed to record levels.
The Trump administration is considering ways to increase domestic diesel supplies, with Energy Secretary Chris Wright contacting executives at major refiners to gauge support for a voluntary restriction on diesel exports, Reuters reported.
The discussions come after reports of a possible 90-day export ban, which the White House has denied.

full_text:
U.S. stocks end flat as traders grapple with hawkish Fed, surge in oil and yields
Investing.com -- Gold prices were little changed on Friday, remaining on track for a weekly decline of more than 3%, as elevated energy prices and rising U.S. Treasury yields kept expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes in focus.
At 23:41 ET (03:41 GMT), XAU/USD was little changed at $4,274.89 an ounce, while Gold Futures rose 0.3% to $4,309.72. XAG/USD fell 0.1% to $63.79, while XPT/USD slipped 0.1% to $1,754.17. The U.S. Dollar Index rose 0.1% to 101.29.
Hormuz uncertainty keeps oil, inflation risks in focus
Oil prices steadied after surging Thursday as the U.S. and Iran remained at an impasse over reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy supplies.
Negotiators were reportedly exploring a phased agreement that would allow Tehran to reopen the waterway while Washington lifts a port blockade. The prospect of disruption to energy flows has kept oil prices elevated and raised concerns that higher fuel costs could slow the pace of inflation easing.
That has become an important driver for gold, as investors assess whether renewed energy price pressures could force the Fed to tighten policy further after last week’s rate increase, its first hike in three years.
Higher interest rates and bond yields generally weigh on gold because the metal does not offer interest income. U.S. Treasury yields rose sharply Thursday, with the 30 year yield approaching 5.5%, its highest level in more than two decades.
The rise has also fuelled concerns that elevated borrowing costs could persist for longer, adding to pressure on non yielding assets.
Investment demand remains resilient despite macro pressure
ANZ analysts said investment demand has stayed resilient, with no material liquidation so far despite increasingly challenging macroeconomic conditions.
That suggests the recent decline has not yet triggered a broad retreat from gold investment positions.
Still, the near term direction remains closely tied to oil prices, Treasury yields and expectations for the Fed’s next moves.
A further rise in energy costs could keep inflation concerns elevated, while higher yields and a stronger dollar would add to the pressure on gold.

title: Analysis-Japan’s bond ’falling knife’ stalls repatriation rush
full_text:
U.S. stocks end flat as traders grapple with hawkish Fed, surge in oil and yields
SINGAPORE, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The tide of Japanese money returning home has begun, but a much larger repatriation of overseas assets is being held back by uncertainty over where Japanese bond yields will peak and how much further the central bank will have to raise interest rates.
The Bank of Japan has likely done enough for now to ward off another wave of speculative bets against the currency, with a rate hike last week, pledges to tackle inflation and, reportedly, a rate check in the foreign exchange market.
Yet major investors remain reluctant to commit heavily to domestic bonds while yields are still climbing and policymakers offer few clues about how much further rates must rise. Two dovish dissenting votes at last week’s meeting and a further selloff in bonds this week only reinforced the uncertainty.
That caution is slowing capital repatriation, leaving one of the world’s biggest pools of overseas capital largely parked abroad for now and capping the scope for a sustained yen rally with potentially far-reaching effects across global markets.
"The fast-money carry trade has already been unwound; the slow-money one has not started," said Shoki Omori, fixed income strategist at Deutsche Bank in Tokyo.
"What is left is structural: Japanese pensions... and households holding overseas assets unhedged," which for the yen means the era of relentless declines may be over, but a durable strengthening trend has yet to begin.
The yen has given up most of its sharp gains from early September and traded near 159 per dollar on Friday, not far from the 157 level, which is the median six-month projection of analysts polled by Reuters earlier this month.
The move leaves the yen down only about 1% for the year, though after years of losses it touched a near four-decade low in July just short of 164 per dollar.
Data shows short sellers have retreated in tandem with the price, with speculative positioning in the yen flipping from a deep net short to the largest net long since July 2025 at $9.7 billion in just the first two weeks of September.
Another challenge for the yen, analysts say, is that major central banks have almost all begun raising rates to tackle inflationary pressure from the Middle East war, suggesting interest-rate differentials with Japan are unlikely to narrow soon.
’NOBODY WANTS TO CATCH THE FALLING KNIFE’
The bond maths keeping more Japanese money at home is simple: benchmark 10-year JGB yields have surged two percentage points in under two years to a 30-year high above 3%, eroding the appeal of overseas debt.
A hedged Treasury position pays a Japanese investor less than domestic bonds, according to Deutsche’s Omori.
Investors bought 4.8 trillion yen of sovereign debt last month, the largest net purchase in three months, according to Barclays’ analysis of Japan Securities Dealers Association data, with banks and insurers among the buyers.
HSBC estimates Japanese banks have sold about $70 billion of foreign bonds this year, versus purchases of $35 billion last year, a retreat felt across markets from Europe to Australia.
Yet life insurers, which hold 438.6 trillion yen ($2.78 trillion) in assets, move slowly and the scale of any allocation shift there is not clear from broad portfolio figures published by the Life Insurance Association of Japan.
"It’s early stage in terms of Japanese repatriating," said Aaron Hurd, senior portfolio manager in the currency group at State Street Global Advisors.
"I think the repatriation story can start to pick up steam in 2027," he said. "It is very important for investors to get some sense that Japanese yields have put in their high. Nobody wants to catch the falling knife."
That calculus could change quickly. Japan’s finance minister has encouraged the $1.8 trillion Government Pension Investment Fund to increase allocations to local markets, and analysts say a pivot by the fund could spur others to do the same.
"If the GPIF makes it official, or we see the hard data, that domestic JGB allocation actually went up ... it’s going to force the other domestic investors to also make changes to their domestic allocations, if they haven’t already," said Paresh Upadhyaya, director of market strategy at Pioneer Investments.
Still, as US yields rise alongside expectations of further tightening by the Federal Reserve, the BOJ may struggle to keep pace or drive a sustained yen rally.
"Until that stabilises it’s probably not a good time for the BOJ to make another move on the hawkish side, or for the currency market to unwind dollar/yen positions," said Naka Matsuzawa, chief macro strategist at Nomura Securities.
"What we need is someone like lifers, starting to see the end of (interest rate) neutralisation by BOJ and start to repatriate their money - that could cause the yen to go higher than 150, I think. But it’s not time for that."

title: SoftBank shares fall as Oracle data-center warning fuels AI funding fears
full_text:
U.S. stocks end flat as traders grapple with hawkish Fed, surge in oil and yields
Investing.com -- SoftBank Group shares pared earlier losses on Friday after Oracle's move to protect itself against potential delays at a major New Mexico data-center project raised fresh concerns over the financing and execution of the AI infrastructure buildout.
The stock had fallen nearly 3% in early Tokyo trading after Oracle disclosed a force-majeure notice to a Blue Owl unit developing Project Jupiter, although SoftBank shares later pared the move. Shares are trading little changed.
Oracle issued the notice over potential delays in securing power for Project Jupiter, a large data-center campus that is part of Stargate, the $500 billion AI infrastructure initiative involving Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank Group.
Oracle is seeking to protect itself from payment obligations if the project is delayed and fails to come online in 2028 as planned, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters and Bloomberg.
The development has raised broader questions over whether the huge amounts of capital being committed to AI infrastructure can be deployed on schedule, particularly as developers face constraints around power, construction and financing, according to Reuters.
The timing is particularly sensitive for SoftBank Group, which has been increasing its leverage to finance its AI strategy. The company raised $11.1 billion through dollar- and euro-denominated bonds this week, with the proceeds aimed in part at funding its investment in OpenAI.
The Oracle development comes as credit investors become more selective toward AI-related debt. Reuters reported that spreads on AI-linked bonds had widened to about 115 basis points, versus 78 basis points for the broader market, while hyperscaler debt issuance is expected to rise sharply as companies finance data centers and chips.
SoftBank's exposure also extends into AI power and infrastructure through SB Energy, which is preparing a potential U.S. listing. Reuters has highlighted the company's $430 billion data-center backlog, while noting that its contracted capacity is concentrated among SoftBank and OpenAI and that much of the backlog is long-dated.

title: European equities edge higher as easing crude overshadow yield spikes
full_text:
Bond market selloff; Costco earnings - what’s moving markets
Investing.com - European equities snapped back on Friday, recovering from a near one-week low in the prior session as a 1% drop in crude oil prices offered relief to energy-intensive sectors and rate-sensitive growth stocks.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index rose 0.7%, positioning the benchmark to wrap up the week with a modest 0.15% gain. If the advances hold through the close, the index will successfully snap a three-week losing streak, providing a brief respite for allocators navigating one of the most volatile months of the year.
Germany’s DAX rose 0.8% ,while France’s CAC 40 and London’s FTSE 100 rose 0.5% each. Italy’s FTSE MIB jumped 1%.
Yet the index remains weighed down on a monthly basis by an avalanche of global rate-hike bets, a 12-point European gas storage deficit, and unresolved Middle-East trade friction.
Corporate earnings hold up under yield shadow
A handful of upbeat corporate earnings and positive single-stock catalysts provided the primary anchor holding continental bourses in the green this week.
The corporate earnings resilience helped offset a brutal rout in fixed-income bourses, where sovereign bond yields across the U.S. and Europe surged to multi-year and multi-decade peaks amid expectations of persistent central bank tightening.
The intraday pull-back in oil futures proved particularly helpful for travel, leisure, and industrial listings, which had been battered earlier in the week by cost-push inflation fears.
"I would give sustained energy relief time to feed through to prices, then assess. Before supporting another hike, you really would want a clear case that existing policy is insufficient to bring underlying inflation down," said Luke Davis, founder and chief market strategist at Bull Market Blueprint.
Eyes on Washington summit and middle east headlines
Despite the Friday bounce, market participants are keeping cash buffers elevated as they digest broader geopolitical signals:
In Washington, investors are parsing initial headlines from the high-stakes summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Markets are seeking concrete signs of progress on trade relations, rare-earth supply chains, and technology export guidelines to ensure the ongoing trade truce remains intact.
"Breakthroughs on long-standing disputes are unlikely, but the meeting could still be a symbolic step forward for future trade talks," said Lukman Otunuga, head of market research at global trading broker FXTM.
Concurrently, energy and foreign exchange bourses remain hyper-sensitive to any diplomatic developments in the Middle East.
While oil prices eased on the day, traders are maintaining a cautious stance, balancing temporary price pullbacks against the potential for renewed supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf and persistent deficits across European natural gas storage.

By Makiko Yamazaki
TOKYO, Sept 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump raised concern about yen weakness during a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said, offering an unusually detailed account of the leaders’ talks on currencies.
"At the recent Japan-US summit meeting, President Trump expressed concern about the yen’s weakness," Katayama said at a regular news conference, adding that she was disclosing the exchange for the first time after consulting with the Prime Minister’s Office.
"Prime Minister Takaichi told him, as a general principle, that an undervalued yen is problematic," Katayama said.
Katayama’s unusually frank account of leaders’ talks, which governments typically keep confidential, points to shared concern in Tokyo and Washington over the yen’s continued slide despite their joint intervention in July.
Takaichi met Trump in New York on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. She later told reporters they had a "timely" discussion about China ahead of Trump’s planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Katayama said the leaders’ discussion on foreign exchange reaffirmed the shared US-Japan stance behind their July 31 coordinated intervention, including a commitment to counter excessive volatility and disorderly moves in the yen.
"In light of this summit meeting, Treasury Secretary (Scott) Bessent and I will continue to communicate closely on a range of matters, including foreign exchange," she said.
The dollar has been rallying against the yen and other major currencies, driven by strong US economic data, a hawkish Federal Reserve and surging US bond yields.
The yen strengthened slightly after Katayama’s remarks, rising from 158.60 per dollar to trade at around 158.
The weak yen is driving up energy import costs that are already elevated due to the US-Israeli war on Iran, fuelling concerns about an inflation overshoot, a headache for Japanese policymakers and for the US, which is worried that a selloff in Japanese bonds could spill over into the Treasury market.
SURGING BOND YIELDS
Katayama declined to comment on whether global rises in government bond yields were discussed at the Japan-US summit.
The benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond yield jumped to a 30-year high of 3.115% on Friday following a steep selloff in the US market.
At a separate news conference, Minoru Kiuchi, the minister in charge of economic revitalisation and an ally of Takaichi’s reflationist camp, said the phase of Abenomics-style reflation policies, with monetary easing and agile fiscal spending, is over.
Kiuchi’s remarks appeared to respond to comments from Bessent, who recently suggested that Japan’s priority should be fighting inflation rather than stimulating growth, signalling concern about what he sees as lingering elements of Abenomics in Takaichi’s policies and among her political allies.
Hirofumi Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp, said remarks by both Katayama and Kiuchi reflected a heightened sense of concern over the yen’s weakness, particularly after Tokyo conducted rate checks on Friday, a move that is often viewed as a precursor to currency intervention.

title: Musk says Colossus 2 data center plans to ramp up Nvidia AI chips by year-end
full_text:
Investing.com-- Elon Musk said early Friday that SpaceXAI plans to roughly double the amount of advanced Nvidia chips used by its Colossus 2 data center by the end of the year.
Musk, in a post on X, said the Memphis, Tennessee- based center used 110,000 of Nvidia’s GB200 chips and 440,000 of Nvidia’s GB300 chips.
The SpaceX CEO– of which SpaceXAI is a unit– said an additional 220,000 GB300 chips will come online by next week and another 220,000 in November.
“If we get lucky, yet another 220k GB300 by late December,” Musk said in response to a post on xAI’s computing capacity.
Musk touts the Colossus center as the “world’s largest AI supercomputer,” with Colossus 1 having been initially built in 2024 to train xAI’s flagship AI Grok.
But the complex has since expanded into providing computing power to other projects. xAI also began renting out computing capacity from the complex to Anthropic and Alphabet’s Google earlier this year.
Musk did not specify whether Colossus 2 had enough readily available capacity and power to run the additional chips.

title: Dollar hits two-month high as Asian currencies weaken, yen nears 160
full_text:
Bond market selloff; Costco earnings - what’s moving markets
Investing.com -- The U.S. dollar held near a two-month high on Friday as rising Treasury yields and expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes supported the greenback, putting renewed pressure on Asian currencies and pushing the Japanese yen toward the closely watched 160-per-dollar level.
The U.S. dollar index was around 101.28, little changed in early Asian trading after rising for a fourth straight day. Its gain slowed to about 0.2% on Thursday from 0.5% on Wednesday, with the index now up about 1.1% this week, matching last week’s pace.
Rising Treasury yields, stronger U.S. economic data and growing expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes continued to support the greenback.
The USD/JPY pair was around 158.46, down 0.3%, after the yen weakened as far as 159.04 on Thursday, its weakest level since September 2. Markets are again watching 160 as a potential test of Japan’s tolerance for further yen weakness.
Dollar gains as yields, rate-hike bets rise
The dollar’s latest advance came alongside a renewed rise in U.S. Treasury yields after economic data pointed to firm activity and persistent price pressures.
The 30-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since June 2004, while the benchmark 10-year yield reached its highest level in nearly two decades.
Weekly initial jobless claims fell by 1,000 to 197,000, below the 201,000 estimate in a Reuters poll, suggesting the labor market is continuing to hold up.
Since the Fed raised rates by 25 basis points last week to 3.75%-4.00%, several officials have indicated that further increases could be needed if inflation fails to moderate. The latest signals have strengthened expectations for another hike.
Oil prices are adding to the inflation pressure. Crude rose almost 4% in volatile trading after a Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia revived concerns over supply disruptions, although gains eased after reports that the U.S. and Iran had discussed reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Yen nears 160 as intervention risk returns
The yen has declined for two weeks following the BOJ’s September 18 policy meeting, when the central bank accelerated its tightening cycle but delivered a decision that included dissent on the board.
Markets viewed the BOJ’s move as insufficiently hawkish relative to the Federal Reserve’s increasingly firm tightening outlook, widening the focus on the gap between U.S. and Japanese rates.
The yen’s decline toward 160 has revived speculation that Japanese authorities could intervene again.
Japan’s return from its holiday has also put the currency back under closer scrutiny as the USD/JPY pair approaches a level that traders have repeatedly watched for signs of official action.
Aussie leads weekly losses, yuan faces PBOC warning
The Australian dollar has been the biggest weekly loser against the U.S. dollar, falling 1.6%, according to DBS.
The currency came under additional pressure after Australia’s unemployment rate rose to 4.6% in August, its highest level since 2021, reducing some of the monetary-policy support for the currency.
The AUD/USD pair was around $0.70, while NZD/USD was near $0.57.
The Chinese yuan also came under renewed pressure. The USD/CNY pair rose for a second day to 6.71, after spending three sessions below 6.70 for the first time since January 2023.
China’s onshore stock and bond markets are closed on Friday for the Mid-Autumn Festival and will reopen on Monday, September 28, while South Korea’s financial markets are also closed Friday for the Chuseok holiday.
Elsewhere, the USD/KRW pair fell 0.3% to 1,361.75, USD/IDR rose 0.3% to 17,930.1, USD/INR was little changed at 96.08, while USD/MYR fell 0.3% to 4.07. The USD/SGD pair was around 1.2791.

title: HelloFresh shares sink 14% after second profit warning
full_text:
Bond market selloff; Costco earnings - what’s moving markets
Investing.com -- HelloFresh shares fell as much as 14.5% on Friday after the German meal-kit company issued its second profit warning of the year, with analysts questioning management’s execution after a sharper-than-planned cut in marketing spending hurt customer acquisition.
HelloFresh late Thursday cut its 2026 revenue outlook to a 9%-11% decline in constant currency, from a previous forecast for a 3%-6% decline and below consensus for a 6.9% fall. It also lowered adjusted EBITDA guidance to €350 million-€370 million from €375 million-€425 million.
The company attributed the downgrade to a larger-than-planned reduction in third-quarter marketing spending, which weighed on new-customer acquisition during the key back-to-school period.
Stifel analyst Clément Genelot retained his “sell” rating, saying the size of the marketing cut raised further questions about HelloFresh’s ability to execute its recovery strategy.
He said the back-to-school campaign was an important test of the company’s execution, with the setback raising questions over its marketing channels, customer targeting and messaging across its meal-kit and ready-to-eat businesses.
HelloFresh expects third-quarter revenue to fall 11%-12% in constant currency, versus consensus for a 6.8% decline. Adjusted EBITDA is expected at €45 million-€55 million, below the €57 million consensus.
Stifel’s €3 price target remains unchanged. Genelot cited continued downside risks to profitability and free cash flow in the absence of clear signs of commercial stabilisation. HelloFresh is due to report third-quarter and nine-month results on Nov. 5.

title: Bitcoin pauses near $84k with focus on rate jitters, Bitget hack
full_text:
Bond market selloff; Costco earnings - what’s moving markets
Investing.com-- Bitcoin moved little on Friday amid pressure from surging Treasury yields, while cryptocurrency markets also watched for the fallout of a major hack targeting exchange Bitget.
The world’s biggest crypto fell 0.1% to $83,999.6 by 02:42 ET (06:41 GMT), and was trading up 3.4% for the week.
Broader crypto prices moved sideways, but were also nursing gains for the week as cheer over favorable U.S. regulations sparked an extended rally in the sector.

Bitget targeted in $352 million hack
Crypto exchange Bitget said late-Thursday it suffered a security breach that affected about $351.6 million in digital assets. The exchange immediately suspended withdrawals, but allowed deposits and trading to continue.
CEO Gracy Chen said investigators found some ties from the breach to a North Korean hacking group, although the perpetrators were not immediately clear.
The company detected unauthorized transfers from some wallets on Thursday afternoon, with affected assets including ether, XRP, USDT, and USDC. Hot and cold wallets were affected in the breach.
The hack is the biggest crypto breach by valuation in 2026. Bitget said the losses were fully covered by its user protection fund of over $464 million.
Soaring yields curb Bitcoin gains
Bitcoin had started the week on strong footing, but sharply curbed gains following a surge in government bond yields.
U.S. 10-year Treasuries surged to levels last seen in 2007 this week, ramping up concerns over rising interest rates and rapidly tightening liquidity conditions. Bond yields across the globe rose in response.
The spike in yields followed a series of hawkish warnings from Federal Reserve officials, who said sticky inflation was likely to invite more rate hikes by the Fed after last week’s 25 basis point raise.
Higher rates bode poorly for crypto, given that they diminish the appeal of investing in volatile, speculative assets with no set yield.
Crypto price today: altcoins drift higher
Broader crypto prices fared slightly better than Bitcoin on Friday, and were trading up for the week.
World no.2 crypto Ether fell 0.4% to $2,674.36, while XRP fell 1.8%.
Solana, Cardano, and BNB rose between 0.1% and 2.5%.
Among memecoins, Dogecoin rose 0.6% and $TRUMP added 2%.

title: AI fears serious, but frontier slowdown unlikely: BMO
full_text:
U.S. stocks end flat as traders grapple with hawkish Fed, surge in oil and yields
Investing.com-- Concerns about artificial intelligence safety were valid, but leading AI labs showed little sign of slowing development, BMO said in a Friday note.
BMO, citing its AI expert, said fears among AI leaders about safety were genuine, given the importance of aligning AI systems with human interests before problems became irreversible.
But the brokerage questioned how committed developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI were to pacing themselves, pointing to their continued releases of increasingly powerful models.
Recent AI-related hacking incidents were largely benign, BMO said. Still, the brokerage warned that bad actors could increasingly exploit open-access models, noting that users had shown an ability to override safeguards and prompt models into misaligned actions.
Get more insights on the AI trade with InvestingPro-- now get up to 50% off
Concerns over AI safety swirled after Anthropic head Dario Amodei called for a coordinated slowdown in frontier development, citing potential risks from the technology to humanity. Several AI executives supported his proposal, with AI safety also being discussed during a U.S.-China summit this week.
BMO expects the U.S. and China to eventually tighten AI regulation, with both countries focusing on open-source and open-access models rather than closed systems.
Such rules would likely require approval before broader public release of open-access models, the expert said. Both governments had incentives to limit AI openness, a shift he said would strengthen pricing power for closed-source frontier labs including Anthropic and OpenAI.
Token prices were expected to keep falling, boosting usage of AI tools, BMO said. However, prices were likely to bottom out around 2030, after which closed-source providers would raise prices as users grew dependent on their tools.
Meta Platforms’ AI positioning had improved due to better use of its AI harness, BMO said. Even so, the company remained behind frontier leaders such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
BMO stayed bullish on AI hardware, citing rising scarcity of computing power as users recognized AI’s capabilities exceeded earlier expectations.
White-collar job displacement was likely to become meaningful by 2028, the. Blue-collar jobs would be affected later, in the 2030s, a delay BMO attributed to Moravec’s Paradox, which holds that tasks requiring physical dexterity are harder for AI to automate than cognitive ones.

title: Nanexa shares rocket 114% on $1.3 billion Novo Nordisk licensing deal
full_text:
Bond market selloff; Costco earnings - what’s moving markets
Investing.com -- Shares of Nanexa surged more than 110% in early Friday trading after the Swedish drug-delivery company announced a global licensing and collaboration agreement with Novo Nordisk worth up to €1.165 billion ($1.3 billion), covering technology aimed at making obesity and diabetes treatments longer-lasting.
Under the deal, Novo Nordisk secures an exclusive worldwide license to Nanexa’s PharmaShell platform, an atomic layer deposition-based drug delivery technology, for use in up to five development programs targeting obesity, type 2 diabetes and other cardiometabolic conditions.
The deal was announced after U.S. market hours on Thursday.
The collaboration aims to produce long-acting injectable formulations that could allow monthly or quarterly dosing, a shift from the weekly injections currently used for many treatments in this category.
Nanexa is eligible to receive total payments of up to €1.165 billion, including €615 million tied to upfront payments and development and regulatory milestones. The remaining consideration is linked to sales milestones. Nanexa will also receive low-single-digit royalties on global net sales of any products that emerge from the partnership.
Novo Nordisk will lead global development and commercialization of any resulting therapies.
"The collaboration brings together Nanexa’s ALD-based long-acting injectable drug delivery platform and Novo’s expertise in obesity and type 2 diabetes treatments," Nanexa said in the press release.
PharmaShell is Nanexa’s proprietary atomic layer deposition drug delivery platform, using an ultra-thin inorganic coating on individual drug particles to enable controlled, sustained release of active pharmaceutical ingredients.

title: Kerry upgraded as Citi sees returns-led upside in ingredients
full_text:
Bond market selloff; Costco earnings - what’s moving markets
Investing.com -- Kerry Group was upgraded to "buy" by a broker, which said improving returns across European ingredients companies could support a recovery in the sector's valuation and restore their longer-term compounder characteristics.
Citi set a €102 price target for Kerry, saying the company appears fundamentally undervalued given its capital efficiency, strong cash conversion and improving earnings trajectory.
The brokerage said its returns-based review of the sector pointed to further upside as growth returns following a volatile post-Covid period.
Citi said investor confidence in European ingredients businesses had weakened after the sector's volatile performance following the pandemic, but argued that underlying franchise quality remains strong.
It singled out Novonesis as the leading reinvestment-driven compounder, while saying Kerry's combination of capital efficiency, cash generation and earnings recovery made its valuation difficult to justify relative to its fundamentals.
Symrise was also highlighted for broad-based improvement in returns that the broker believes is not fully reflected in its valuation. DSM-Firmenich, meanwhile, was described as having significant recovery potential, although execution remains an important factor.
The brokerage said Givaudan's strong returns and cash conversion are already well reflected in its valuation, while Croda still needs to demonstrate further progress in its operational turnaround.
The report argues that a returns-based approach provides a better way of assessing the quality of the European ingredients sector than simply focusing on near-term earnings growth, with improvements in capital efficiency potentially supporting a renewed recovery in valuations.
